## Our Codesigner

Our codesigner’s name is Lily Lloyd, she’s a sophomore at Garnet Valley High School and a close friend of ours. In her free time, she likes to read books and crochet.   
At 6 years old she was diagnosed with Specific Learning Disability Reading and Specific Learning Disability Spelling. With phonological and orthographic dyslexia, she struggles to convert letters on a paper or screen into cohesive words, as well as the breaking down of certain syllables and sounds. This affects her academic experience greatly, as she is a high-achieving student who takes many rigorous courses.

## Needs and Requirements

| Needs | Product Requirements |
| :---- | :---- |
| Works on a computer | The device will not be physical, but based on software for computer use |
| Works for the websites she uses the most (online textbook, Schoology, etc.) | The device will be able to adjust these specific websites |
| Change the text size and font | The device will have a slider and buttons to change text size and font |
| Change the overlay color | The device will have buttons to change the color of the overlay. |

## Concept Generation

As we looked at Lily’s needs, we knew our project had to be digital. With the amount of time Lily spends on her computer, we decided that coded software was out best choice. Looking at the parameters, one concept stood out to us: a Chrome extension.   
We first searched the Chrome web store with Lily to find any already existing solutions that we could alter to suit Lily and her needs specifically. We found several extensions such as ‘Dyslex.ie’ and ‘Dyslexia friendly’ which offered tools to make navigating the web easier for dyslexic people. After testing them with Lily, we found some features that Lily liked the most. 

*These were:* 

- The ability to change the font and text size  
- The ability to change the overlay color  
- An option to turn the extension off

We then did research on how to code an extension. It required knowledge of Javascript, HTML, and CSS, which we had, however we still had to learn a bit more on the process of building an extension itself.

- We did this through analysis of existing source codes.

**Iteration 1: Low-Fidelity Prototype**  
Before coding we needed an initial sketch, to figure out what we needed to get done. This was our low-fidelity prototype.

We went to Canva and drew what we wanted the extension to look like. We also created a flow chart and overall plan so we could stay on task as we progressed. After showing this to Lily, we went ahead and started coding.   
**Iteration 2: High-Fidelity Prototype**  
We downloaded Visual Studio code on a windows device and began the coding process. It worked on both dark and light modes, as we wanted Lily to have preference and choice.

[Screen Recording 2024-03-31 at 6.00.11 PM.mov](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1Jo07lCBrBCYqF9RtpyehaWaxRLw0LcBa/view?usp=sharing): Video/Testing Link

*Software Tools:*  
We primarily used Visual Studio Code to code in HTML, CSS, and Javascript.

*Build Instructions:*  
To create a Chrome extension, a manifest.json must first be created so that Chrome can identify the code as an extension. Next, you will need to add an action that allows the default program to display a popup, as this will be the control panel of our extension. If desired, an image can be chosen to use as a logo. For this, upload 3 images of sizes, 128, 32, and 16 pixels so it may be seen on many devices. Back to the extension itself, pre-made CSS files can be downloaded and uploaded into the file, or they can be hand-made. We used the bulma.min.css framework for this particular project. We then used HTML to physically manifest our buttons, sliders, and radios(smaller circular buttons). After the design was complete, the last step is to code the extension using JavaScript. Some fonts may be included with the software you use, however, more niche scripts such as OpenDyslexic (which we needed) must be downloaded, converted, and then represented into the code. Through collected all the data we had coded within the extension, we were able to manipulate it just as we needed, thus creating our final project.

## Testing

**Test Plan:**  
To test the extension, we first did some basic testing within our group to make sure there were no syntax, runtime, or other code errors. Then we gave the extension to Lily for her to try out and assessed her approval of our work.    
After getting feedback, we made the necessary adjustments. Apart from altering code, there was a fair amount of behind-the-scenes research work to better understand our goals and how to achieve them.   
Learning and experimentation was a hige part of the process, and as difficult as it was, we found this experience to be exhilarating and highly rewarding.

**Testing Results:**  
*Successes:*

- Have working buttons and sliders  
- Getting the fonts to change within the extension when the buttons were clicked  
    
  *Failures:*  
- Using our extension on websites due to security issues  
- Coding for the functionality of all features made in CSS & HTML

## Reflections

**What we learned:**  
During this process, we learned a lot about what goes into coding and designing. We learned how to effectively design a product, starting with sketches, and prototypes, and then moving to the final product. We also learned about the sheer dedication and commitment that goes into many of the extensions and websites we use today. Moreover, we learned that time management is vital and asking for help should not be a last resort. There are many things we wished we did differently, but overall, we truly enjoyed this challenge.

**Scalability:**  
	Around 1 in 10 people have dyslexia according to Discovery ABA, and according to Yale, it affects 80-90% of those with learning disabilities. Since many people in the world share this issue, it’s applicable to many others, however our extension is tailored to Lily. But since our product is also customizable and easily accessible on the internet, many people can utilize it. After we fix our security issues, we are planning to release it on the Chrome Web Store for free. That way, anyone that has chrome will be able to access our product. 

**Improvements:**  
The biggest improvement that we could make was getting all of our features to work as planned. Unfortunately due to the multitude of security issues, we were not able to create a fully working extension in the given time. We also did not add the feature of turning everything on or off. However, we hope to continue with our plan and overcome the issues we faced to present Lily with a wonderful asset to her school experience.
